THE QUALIFIER IS LOAD-BEARING. Bunge refuses this case because ordering is not bonding, not
because the members are events. The refusal runs through his whole apparatus: an aggregate is
a collection "not held together by bonds" (ch. 1 p. 4), Definition 1.1 requires the members
CONNECTED — where a connection, unlike a mere relation "such as that of being older", has at
least one relatum acting on the other (Sec. 1.2) — and Definition 1.2(iii) carries the
nonempty-bondage condition 𝔅_A(σ,t) ≠ ∅ into every system's structure. A shelf of books
ordered by author carries a relation and no bonds. "Unconnected" in the label is Definition
1.1's own word; a plainer "an ordered collection" would understate the disagreement and invite
the reply that he was only excluding events.

openDecisions.title: D2 — Intensional targets, and the `is_about` question
openDecisions.problem: **The current design.** `cco:ont00001808` (`is_about`) is never asserted on an entry, enforced by `shapes/atlas-shapes.ttl`. Rationale in README: it keeps the catalogue neutral between realist (Bunge) and constructivist (Klir) traditions.
openDecisions.fix: **Candidate fix — assert `is_about`, with tradition-appropriate targets.** BFO has no `Concept` class by design, but an ICE may be about another ICE, since generically dependent continuants are Entities. So Klir's definition targets a *construct*; Bunge's targets concrete things in Θ, which his own text states. The realist/constructivist split stops being a silence and becomes the atlas's most interesting queryable field.

openDecisions.title: D3 — The architectural fork: annotation spine vs computable representation
openDecisions.problem: **The fork.** Either (A) the OWL layer is an auditable annotation and citation spine, with census and independence living in Lean; or (B) structure goes into the representation so relations between definitions can actually be computed here.
openDecisions.fix: **Trigger: encode Myers, then decide.** Not a headcount. Myers' deterministic system is interpretable "in any cartesian category" — schematic, not about any particular subject matter. Klir targets a construct, Bunge targets concrete things, and Myers arguably targets nothing in particular. That is exactly where D2's target-typing either works or visibly breaks, and one entry settles more than ten would.

openDecisions.title: D6 — BFO/CCO alignment vs a bibliographic ontology
openDecisions.problem: Both councils recommended dropping BFO/CCO for FaBiO or FRBR, on the grounds that the alignment currently buys nothing computational. Technically fair, and FRBR's Work/Expression/Manifestation would directly address the GDC identity problem below.
openDecisions.fix: **Held anyway**, for a reason the councils could not price: the alignment was asked about by name, by a professional semantic engineer whose interest shaped this project's form. It is relationship-bearing as well as technical, and re-parenting three entries later is cheap.

# Shape Category for Klir's S = (T, R)

The *shape category* `I_Klir` encodes the dependency structure of Klir's
system definition S = (T, R) (Facets of Systems Science, 2001, Eq. 1.1).

This is the simplest non-discrete shape category in the landscape:
2 objects and 1 generating arrow. It is the common ancestor of both
Bunge's CES triple and Mobus's 8-tuple — the `rfl` proofs of the
commuting triangle trace to both authors inheriting T as `Set α` and
R as `Set (α × α)` from Klir without changing the mathematical type.

## Construction

- `things`: T — the set of things (thinghood)
- `relation`: R — the set of relations on T (systemhood)
- `relation_on_things`: R → T — R is defined over T

A thing becomes a system when you specify which of its parts are related.
The single arrow captures this: the relation DEPENDS on the things.

# Shape Category for Bunge's CES Framework

The *shape category* `I_Bunge` encodes the dependency structure of Bunge's
system definition σ = ⟨C, E, S⟩ (Treatise on Basic Philosophy Vol. 4, Def 1.2, 1979).

## Construction

We define a quiver with 3 vertices (the tuple positions) and 3 generating arrows
(the structural dependencies), then take the free category via `Paths`.

## Arrow Direction Convention

Arrows point from the *dependent* to what it *depends on*. This makes a system-as-diagram
(a functor from the shape category to a data category) covariant.

- S → C: structure is defined over composition
- S → E: structure is defined over environment
- E → C: environment acts on composition (Bunge's interaction axiom)

# Shape Category for Bertalanffy's General System Theory

The *shape category* `I_Bertalanffy` encodes the dependency structure of Bertalanffy's
verbal definition of "system".

## Source

Bertalanffy (1968), *General System Theory*, ch. 3 "Some System Concepts", p. 55:

> "A system can be defined as a complex of interacting elements. Interaction means that
> elements, p, stand in relations, R, so that the behavior of an element p in R is different
> from its behavior in another relation, R'."

Two positions are named in that sentence — the elements `p` and the relations `R` — and one
dependency: the relations are *on* the elements.

## Arrow direction — DECLARED, not assumed

`interrelation_on_elements : interrelation ⟶ elements`, read aloud: **"the interrelation
depends on the elements"** — you cannot state R without already having the p's it holds
between. This is the same convention as every other shape in this development (Klir's
`relation_on_things`, Mobus's `network_on_components`): an arrow points from the dependent
position to the position it depends on. It is NOT a function arrow and NOT a flow arrow.

## What this shape does NOT capture — the predicate gap

Bertalanffy's interaction clause carries a condition Klir's `S = (T, R)` does not: the
behaviour of an element **must differ** across relations. That is a predicate constraining
which R qualify, not a position and not a dependency, so the quiver cannot express it and
`bertalanffyToKlir` below discards it. The two definitions therefore have isomorphic shapes
(`shapeIso`) while making *different* demands — the shape functor is not injective on
definitional content.

This is a limit of the shape method, exhibited rather than asserted: `shapeIso` proves the
structures correspond, and this paragraph names exactly what survives the correspondence and
what does not. Compare Bunge's near-identical difference-making test — "unlike a mere
relation, a connection makes some difference to its relata" (1979, ch. 1 §1.2) — which Bunge
*does* promote to definitional force via the nonempty-bondage requirement, and which
`ShapeBunge` likewise cannot see.

## The 1972 restatement is a different shape

Bertalanffy (1972), "The History and Status of General Systems Theory", *Academy of
Management Journal* 15(4), p. 417, adds a third position:

> "A system may be defined as a set of elements standing in interrelation among themselves
> **and with the environment**."

That definition would carry a second arrow (`interrelation ⟶ environment`) and is deliberately
NOT encoded here — this file is the 1968 shape. The 1968 → 1972 pair is a definition revising
itself, and the two shapes are the record of what the revision changed.

positions.doc: what they also stand in interrelation *with*

# Shape Category for Mobus's 8-Tuple Framework

The *shape category* `I_Mobus` encodes the dependency structure of Mobus's
system definition S = (C, N, E, G, B, T, H, Δt).

## Construction

We define a quiver with 8 vertices (the tuple positions) and 5 generating arrows
(derived from the coherence constraints in `MobusSystem`), then take the free category.

## Arrow Provenance

Each generating arrow traces to a specific coherence constraint:
- `network_on_components` ← `network_components : N.nodes = C`
- `interfaces_in_components` ← `interfaces_sub : B.interfaces ⊆ C`
- `external_on_env` ← `externalFlows_nodes` (environment component)
- `external_on_boundary` ← `externalFlows_nodes` (boundary component)
- `env_disjoint_comp` ← `disjoint : C ∩ E.objects = ∅`

## Isolated Vertices

`transforms`, `history`, and `timeScale` have no generating arrows. They are
parametric data with no structural role in the coherence constraints.

The common-sense definition of a system, expressed by Eq. (1.1), is rather
primitive. This, paradoxically, is its weakness as well as its strength. The definition
is weak because it is too general and, consequently, of little pragmatic value. It is
strong because it encompasses all other, more specific definitions of systems. In
this regard, this most general definition of systems provides us with a criterion by
which we can determine whether any given object is a system or not: an object is
a system if and only if it can be described in a form that conforms to Eq. (1.1).
For example, a collection of books is not a system, only a set. However, when
we organize the books in some way, the collection becomes a system. When we
order them, for instance, by authors' names, we obtain a system since any ordering
of a set is a relation defined on the set.

where i and l are indexes. The index i is a subsystem index and the index l is the level of organization in the system-subsystem hierarchy. Both are 0 for the initial system of interest, S 0,0 is the designated SOI.
context.after:
Recall from the previous chapter that the ontological framework specified that the SOI be designated as level 0 . This will make sense in this definition as we show how the system definition leads to a natural way to deconstruct the component/interaction level ( +1 ) in the framework. Several later chapters in the book will describe the application of these equations (and the knowledgebase described in Chap. 8) to even more complex adaptive and evolvable systems (CAESs) described in Part III.

 
 As we will see later, we will actually incorporate both indexes into a single coding scheme that will give both the level in the hierarchy and the component index using a 'dotted' numbering scheme. This will be conducive to providing key values for the knowledgebase schema to be covered in Chap.

context.before:
That formulation, however, treated a system as being essentially static over its duration. That is, the system would not change over its life time. Additionally, the formulation only minimally represented the environment of a system. In this paper we seek to revise the model to enhance the handling of environmental aspects and to extend the model’s ability to represent a full life-cycle of any instance of any kind of system.

## Extending and Modifying the Framework

We begin with a basic revision of the original 7-tuple structure, reproduced here.

###### Si,l=〈C,N,G,B,T,H,∆t〉i,l The original Eq. 4.1 in (Mobus, 2022).
context.match:
Revised Eq. 4.1 is as follows.

###### Si,l=〈C,N,E,G,B,T,H,∆t〉i,l (1)

In what follows, the subscript indexes, i, for index number in the set, and l, for level in the complexity/organization hierarchy will be dropped for simplicity.

S is now given as an oct-tuple with new member E containing the set, O, (standing for “objects” in the environment that are sources and sinks in a unified set) and a new object, M, containing the non-point source/sink variables constituting the interacting milieu around the system.
context.after:
Examples of a milieu are given below. The set O subsumes the sets, Src and Snk which were included in the original G bipartite network and were effectively ‘hidden’ from exposure of the model. This was deemed an unnecessary complexity, particularly since many objects in a system’s environment may be both sources and sinks simultaneously (for background, refer to Mobus, 2022). The environment object is now defined as:

E= 〈O,M〉 

O= 〈o0,o1,o2,…ok,…om〉 

Where O is the set of object sources and sinks in the environment of the SOI.

The milieu is represented by the abstract M object. M is the set of variables that are part of the environment but do not have a discrete (point) source. They surround or ‘bathe’ the system in conditions that impact or influence the state of the system, but do not interact necessarily through a discrete set of interfaces, as in the case of flows.

entries.label: Klir (2001), Facets of Systems Science, eq. (1.1)
entries.verbatim:
S = (T, R),   (1.1)

where S, T, R denote, respectively, a system, a set of things distinguished within S, and a relation (or, possibly, a set of relations) defined on T. Clearly, the thinghood and systemhood properties of S reside in T and R, respectively.
entries.displayContext: where S, T, R denote, respectively, a system, a set of things distinguished within S, and a relation (or, possibly, a set of relations) defined on T.

annotation.title: VERIFIED
annotation.body: verbatim transcribed from the primary text, not paraphrased.

annotation.title: DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED
annotation.body:
cco:ont00001808 (is about). Klir is an avowed
constructivist — on his account the relation R is defined by the modeller, not
discovered. Asserting what this definition is *about* would commit the catalogue
to a realist reading Klir does not hold. The neutrality is the point.

annotation.title: EXAMPLES NOTE
annotation.body:
Klir gives no excluded example in Bunge's sense. His "a collection
of books is not a system, only a set" (p. 5, same paragraph as the included
examples) is the opening move of an argument whose conclusion is that organising
it *makes* it one, and on his own criterion — an object is a system iff it CAN BE
DESCRIBED in a form conforming to Eq. (1.1) — a bare collection is not refused but
merely not yet distinguished. Recording it as atlas:excludedExample would give it
the same form as Bunge's ontic refusal at Definition 1.1 and manufacture a symmetry
the two authors do not share; in a cases matrix it would read as agreement where
the finding is the opposite. The three included examples are grouped as Klir groups
them: his "etc." marks the variants as instances of a kind, not an enumeration of
cases. Source read 2026-08-03; see docs/proposals/P1-klir-examples.md and
docs/proposals/P3-stance-axes.md.

annotation.title: CENSUS NOTE
annotation.body:
Klir's own gloss splits the definition's two slots into named
properties — thinghood in T, systemhood in R. Recorded as separate primitives
rather than folded into `thing` and `relation`, because whether they are distinct
primitives is a question the census should answer, not one the encoding should
prejudge.

annotation.title: ADJACENT MATERIAL, NOT YET ENTERED
annotation.body:
Klir's self-assessment on the same page (the
definition is "too general and, consequently, of little pragmatic value" but
"encompasses all other, more specific definitions of systems") is a claim ABOUT
this definition's relation to others. It belongs in the mapping layer, not in
this entry.

annotation.title: NEXT TIER
annotation.body:
the dependency quiver (tier 1) for this definition already exists in
Lean as ShapeKlir in systems-science-foundations. The two encodings must be
checked against each other before either is cited.

entries.label: Bunge (1979), general characterisation: σ = ⟨C, E, S⟩
entries.sourceLocation: ch. 1, §1.1 (the general concept of a system)
entries.verbatim: One way of characterizing the general concept of a system is this. Let T be a nonempty set. Then the ordered triple σ = ⟨C, E, S⟩ is (or represents) a system over T iff C and E are mutually disjoint subsets of T (i.e. C ∩ E = ∅), and S is a nonempty set of relations on the union of C and E. The system is conceptual if T is a set of conceptual items, and concrete (or material) if T ⊆ Θ is a set of concrete entities, i.e. things.
entries.displayContext: C and E are mutually disjoint subsets of T (i.e. C ∩ E = ∅), and S is a nonempty set of relations on the union of C and E.
entries.authorCaveat: However, the preceding is not a definition proper, because it does not tell us what exactly is the membership of the coordinates C, E and S of the ordered triple. We must therefore define the notions of composition, environment, and structure of a thing.

annotation.body:
"is (or represents)". Bunge's own parenthetical hedges between the triple
BEING a system and REPRESENTING one, and he resolves it later in the same chapter
by calling the triple "the minimal model of system σ at time t". This is direct
primary-text evidence on the is-versus-represents question — the distinction the
Lean encodings do not type. Klir's (T,R) IS the system; Bunge's ⟨C,E,S⟩ is a model
OF a thing. Same shape, different ontological status.

NOT the same triple as the informal gloss. The fuller form Bunge actually works
with is relativised to a class A of things and indexed by time: s_A(σ,t) =
⟨𝒞_A(σ,t), ℰ_A(σ,t), 𝒮_A(σ,t)⟩. Anyone citing "Bunge's CES triple" as a bare
3-tuple is citing the informal version.

annotation.title: CES, NOT CESM
annotation.body:
Mechanism is not a coordinate here. The string "CESM" does not
occur in the 1979 text; mechanism becomes central in later Bunge (see How Does It
Work, 2004). Any citation pairing "1979" with "CESM" is an anachronism.

annotation.title: DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED
annotation.body:
cco:ont00001808 (is about). Bunge is a realist and
would endorse the reading; asserting it anyway would still break the catalogue's
neutrality, which must not depend on which tradition an entry belongs to.

entries.label: Bunge (1979), Definition 1.1: concrete system
entries.verbatim: DEFINITION 1.1 An object is a concrete system iff it is composed of at least two different connected things.
entries.displayForm: An object is a concrete system iff it is composed of at least two different connected things.

annotation.title: THE SEPARATING INSTANCE, IN BUNGE'S OWN WORDS
annotation.body:
His excluded example is
"a collection of events, EVEN IF ORDERED". Klir, on the passage recorded in entry
001, holds that ordering a collection is exactly what makes it a system: "any
ordering of a set is a relation defined on the set". Two founders, both verbatim,
disagreeing about whether an ordered collection is a system. This is the highest-
value datum in the catalogue so far and it was found by reading, not by inference.

annotation.title: MACHINERY BEHIND THE REFUSAL
annotation.body:
(Definition 1.2, encoded here as primitives rather
than as its own entry, because it defines composition/environment/structure and
not "system"):
  𝒞_A(σ,t) = {x ∈ A | x ⊏ σ}
  ℰ_A(σ,t) = {x ∈ A | x ∉ 𝒞_A(σ,t) & ∃y (y ∈ 𝒞_A(σ,t) & (x ▷ y ∨ y ▷ x))}
  𝒮_A(σ,t) = relations, in particular bonds, on 𝒞_A(σ,t) ∪ ℰ_A(σ,t), with the
             bonding set 𝔅_A(σ,t) ≠ ∅
The nonempty-bonding requirement is what does the refusing, and it is encoded in
systems-science-foundations as ConcreteSystem.bondage_nonempty over the ActsOn
class (Bunge's ▷). The two encodings agree; that agreement should be recorded as
a mapping claim once the mapping layer exists, not asserted here.

annotation.title: RELATION TO ENTRY 002
annotation.body:
Bunge presents 002 first and then disowns it as "not a
definition proper". 003 is the definition proper. They are not alternative
phrasings of one claim and must not be merged.

entries.label: Bertalanffy (1972), The History and Status of General Systems Theory, p. 417
entries.verbatim: A system may be defined as a set of elements standing in interrelation among themselves and with the environment. This can be expressed mathematically in different ways.
entries.displayForm: A system may be defined as a set of elements standing in interrelation among themselves and with the environment.
entries.displayContext: This can be expressed mathematically in different ways.
entries.authorCaveat: This can be expressed mathematically in different ways.

annotation.body:
HVP: the page was read against this transcription on 2026-08-05, including
the two things a paraphrase would smooth away — that it prints "may be defined" rather than
"can be", and that "and with the environment" is really there. The second is the clause that
distinguishes this definition from the 1968 book's, so the whole entry turns on it.

annotation.title: WHY THE 1972 ARTICLE AND NOT THE 1968 BOOK
annotation.body:
The book is the canonical
citation, and its ch. 3 (p. 55) gives the same definition verbally — "a complex of interacting
elements" — followed by the differential-equation formalisation, eq. (3.1). The only copy of
the book available to this encoding is an OCR whose ligatures are systematically damaged and
in which **equation (3.1) did not survive at all**. Transcribing a verbatim from it would
violate the catalogue's first discipline. The 1972 article restates the definition in a text
with clean provenance, so it is entered first. The 1968 entry remains wanted, and the pair is
worth having: the definitions differ.

annotation.title: WHAT THE REVISION CHANGED
annotation.body:
1968: "a complex of interacting elements." 1972: "a set of elements
standing in interrelation among themselves AND WITH THE ENVIRONMENT." The environment becomes
constitutive of the definition rather than a later distinction. Encoding both would make that
revision machine-checkable at the shape level — the 1972 shape carries an arrow the 1968 shape
does not.

annotation.title: WHAT IS DELIBERATELY OUT OF THE VERBATIM
annotation.body:
The differential-equation material sits on the
following page (p. 418, "a set of n measures, called state variables... a set of n
simultaneous, first-order differential equations"), and its equation is a page image in this
scan, not extractable text. Including that sentence would end the verbatim on a colon pointing
at something the catalogue does not hold. It is a candidate for a second entry from the same
bearer, in the way Bunge's CES triple and Definition 1.1 are two entries from one book.

THE AUTHOR'S OWN HEDGE is inside the verbatim, not paraphrased around it: "This can be
expressed mathematically in different ways." On the same page he names Mesarović, Maccia,
Ashby and Klir as fellow axiomatisers — the founder pointing at two other entries in this
catalogue.

entries.label: Bertalanffy (1968), General System Theory, eq. (3.1)
entries.verbatim:
A system can be defined mathematically in various ways. For illustration, we choose a system of simultaneous differential equations. Denoting some measure of elements, pᵢ (i = 1, 2, … n), by Qᵢ, these, for a finite number of elements and in the simplest case, will be of the form:

dQ₁/dt = f₁(Q₁, Q₂, … Qₙ)
dQ₂/dt = f₂(Q₁, Q₂, … Qₙ)
⋯
dQₙ/dt = fₙ(Q₁, Q₂, … Qₙ)                                    (3.1)
entries.displayForm:
dQ₁/dt = f₁(Q₁, Q₂, … Qₙ)
dQ₂/dt = f₂(Q₁, Q₂, … Qₙ)
⋯
dQₙ/dt = fₙ(Q₁, Q₂, … Qₙ)
entries.displayContext: For illustration, we choose a system of simultaneous differential equations.
entries.authorCaveat: A system can be defined mathematically in various ways.

annotation.title: HVP, AND THE SCOPE OF THE CHECK IS EXACTLY THIS
annotation.body:
Shingai read the page on
2026-08-05 — the prose against this transcription, and the equation against the page image,
because no text layer in any held source contains eq. (3.1) at all. The equation here is
transcribed from that image, screenshot-verified the same day. The held Kindle text renders
subscript i as t ("pt", "Qt") — an artifact of the rendering, not the book; the subscripts
above are as printed. Page numbering is Kindle print-equivalent pagination, corroborated by
the print index's "mathematical definition, 56-60".

annotation.title: THE HEDGE IS PART OF THE RECORD
annotation.body:
The verbatim opens at "A system can be defined mathematically
in various ways" rather than at the equation: 1968 offers the differential equations as one
illustration among various possible formalisations, and cutting the hedge would harden an
avowedly illustrative choice into a definition the author did not state that way. The 1972
restatement (entry 004) carries the same hedge in the other direction — a verbal definition
pointing at unspecified mathematics.

annotation.title: WHAT THE REVISION CHANGED, NOW CITABLE FROM BOTH ENDS
annotation.body:
1968: elements and their interrelation,
no environment term — the shape has two positions and one arrow, and is proved isomorphic to
Klir's. 1972: "and with the environment" — a third position and a second arrow. The difference
is machine-checked: bert68To72Pre embeds the 1968 shape in the 1972 one (bert68To72_obj_injective),
and environment_is_new proves the environment position is not in its image. This entry is the
1968 end of that pair; mapping 003 (environment-channel.md) is where the finding is stated.

annotation.title: WHY THE 1972 ARTICLE WAS ENTERED FIRST

model-drafted by the P5 pipeline 2026-08-17, checked by
Shingai Thornton 2026-08-18 in a guided session against the vault digitisation — verbatim,
spans, both caveats and their positions, location, primitives and cases each ruled on. Not

annotation.title: DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED
annotation.body:
cco:ont00001808 (is about). The catalogue records that this
author, at this locus, states this definition in these words; what the definition is about
is not asserted, per the neutrality invariant.

annotation.title: NO ENVIRONMENT ELEMENT
annotation.body:
The published tuple has seven coordinates and no E. The revisions
manuscript revises eq. (4.1) to the eight-tuple with environment first-class — the version
the Lean development encodes — and is registered as its own bearer (mobus-book-revisions)
precisely so the revision is citable rather than silently merged. prim:environment is
deliberately NOT invoked here: the row lighting up only at the revisions entry is the census
recording the revision.

annotation.title: PRIMITIVES
annotation.body:
(ruled 2026-08-18, two layers): from the passage itself, the conservative
Bertalanffy-1968 standard — subsystem, level of organization, hierarchy, system of interest,
plus time admitted notationally via Δt, the exact dQᵢ/dt precedent. From the PARTS-HARVEST
run the same day (the Bunge Definition 1.2 rule in docs/adding-an-entry.md): component,
flow network, bipartite flow graph, boundary, transformation rule, memory and time interval —
the author's own words for the tuple's symbols, each scope note carrying his defining
sentence machine-located in §4.3.3's subsections. Five were model-harvested and checked in
the guided pass; transformation rule and time interval were hand-recovered with narrower
spans after the model's wider ones failed the locate gate (display-math furniture).

annotation.title: CASES
annotation.body:
one admit. The steel-plant worked example (§4.5) is HELD, not recorded: the model
proposed it, but its licensing sentence describes the plant without ruling it a system.
It returns if a stronger licensing sentence is found in §4.5. Nothing in the chapter is
refused systemhood.

annotation.title: NEXT TIER
annotation.body:
Systems/Category/ShapeMobus.lean encodes the REVISED eight-tuple (Book-revisions
Eq. 1), not this published seven-tuple. The formalisedAs pointer therefore belongs to the
forthcoming revisions entry, and this entry deliberately carries none.

annotation.title: DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED
annotation.body: cco:ont00001808 (is about), per the neutrality invariant.

annotation.title: THE REVISION IS THE FINDING
annotation.body:
Entry 006's tuple has seven coordinates; this one has eight,
and the new coordinate is E — the environment, now carrying the source/sink objects O and
the milieu M. The environment becoming first-class is the same move Bertalanffy made between
1968 and 1972 (environment_is_new in the Lean development), which makes this the catalogue's
second revision arc with the same content. prim:environment lights up on this entry and not
on entry 006 by design: the census row difference IS the record of the revision.

annotation.title: PRIMITIVES
annotation.body:
(ruled 2026-08-18): the conservative standard, the words of the passage itself —
set, environment, hierarchy, level of organization, object, milieu — plus time notationally
via Δt (the dQᵢ/dt precedent, as on entry 006). "System" is deliberately NOT recorded as a
primitive: it is the definiendum, the term the definition fixes, not an undefined input it
rests on — and a row every entry would trivially share carries no census information.

annotation.title: NO AUTHOR CAVEAT
annotation.body:
(ruled 2026-08-18): the drafted candidate ("the subscript indexes ... will
be dropped for simplicity") is notational bookkeeping, not a self-qualification. The
manuscript's framing sentence — that the 2022 treatment "ignored a critical aspect of real
systems, namely that they age and change" — qualifies the OLD definition, and belongs to
this arc note rather than to a caveat on the new one.

annotation.title: HELD, NOT ENTERED
annotation.body:
the manuscript's lifecycle equations (St+1 = St⟨ΔS⟩ with
ΔS = ⟨ΔC,ΔN,ΔE,ΔG,ΔB,ΔT,ΔH⟩) were scanned as a candidate. They introduce typed components
and fix a transition relation, but they define system CHANGE over an already-given S rather
than the term "system" — held pending a spec §5 ruling. They are the natural formal locus of
the Mobus life-cycle work and the Bunge–Mobus change-convergence thread, and likely enter
through the mapping layer rather than as an entry.

annotation.body:

primitiveSchemeScopeNote:
LEXICAL, NOT SEMANTIC. A primitive here records that an author uses a WORD as
a primitive. Two entries linked to prim:thing are not thereby claimed to mean the same
thing by it — Klir's "thing" is unrestricted, Bunge's ranges over concrete entities in
Theta, and whether those are one primitive or two is a census question this vocabulary
must not prejudge.

The consequence: recurrence counts computed over this scheme are a FIRST-PASS LEXICAL
measure. Semantic co-reference is a mapping-layer claim and owes evidence like any
other. Minting a separate primitive per author would make recurrence trivially zero;
merging them by hand would make it trivially high. Lexical recurrence is the honest
starting point, and its limits are stated here rather than discovered later.

profile.verdict: A taxonomy. Nothing is entailed beyond transitive closure of the asserted tree.
